- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Session transcripts

Every agent session that works on this repository is kept here as evidence.
A session's transcript is the full record of what it read, searched,

#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Updates a clean folder to its remote's main (or REF), the safe way.
#
#   tools/clean-update.sh [--dir DIR] [REF]      (default: this folder, main)
#
# Clean sessions run with git's lazy fetching off (GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1, set
# by config/claude/clean.json), so no command can download a file the clean
# folder leaves out. A checkout of new commits needs lazy fetching for the
# files it does check out, so this script allows it for exactly one
# fast-forward, then re-applies the sparse checkout and checks that no file
# under a spec-side folder (config/spec-side-folders) reached the disk or the
# folder's .git, nor any spec-side file under another branch (the records
# branch keeps spec-side outputs). Stop and tell the owner if it fails.
#
# The fast-forward runs with --no-stat and -q: a merge summary (diffstat)
# counts the lines of every changed file, and with lazy fetching allowed git
# downloads the excluded files' contents to count them.
set -eu

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
if [ "${1:-}" = "--dir" ]; then ROOT=$(cd "$2" && pwd); shift 2; fi
ref=${1:-main}
role=$(cat "$ROOT/.claude/small-beeps-role" 2>/dev/null || true)
[ "$role" = clean ] || { echo "clean-update.sh is for clean folders (role here: ${role:-none})" >&2; exit 2; }

GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" fetch -q origin
env -u GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH git -C "$ROOT" merge -q --no-stat --ff-only "origin/$ref"
GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 sh "$ROOT/tools/clean-setup.sh" > /dev/null

# The spec-side folders, from the one list (since M3).
SPEC_FOLDERS=$(grep -v '^#' "$ROOT/config/spec-side-folders" | cut -f1)
[ -n "$SPEC_FOLDERS" ] || { echo "STOP: no spec-side folders in config/spec-side-folders"; exit 1; }
# Any path with one of them, or a spec-experiments/ folder, in it.
SPEC_RE="(^|/)(spec-experiments|$(printf '%s\n' "$SPEC_FOLDERS" | paste -sd '|' -))/"
fail=0
for p in $SPEC_FOLDERS; do
    [ ! -e "$ROOT/$p" ] || { echo "STOP: $p is on disk"; fail=1; }
    have=$(GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" ls-tree -r HEAD -- "$p" | awk '$2 == "blob" { print $3 }' \
        | GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" cat-file --batch-check='%(objectname)' 2>/dev/null | grep -vc missing || true)
    [ "$have" = 0 ] || { echo "STOP: $have file(s) under $p are in .git"; fail=1; }
done
# Spec-side outputs can reach .git another way: each record on the records
# branch keeps fwtest's own and the spec experiments' outputs, and fetching
# a record's files wholesale brings their blobs in (it happened once, in
# M1; docs/EXPOSURE.md). So under every branch, remote branch included, a
# file under a folder named spec-experiments/ or as a spec-side folder, at
# any depth, must be missing too.
# Trees are in a blob-less clone, so this reads no file.
have=$(GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" for-each-ref --format='%(objectname)' refs/heads refs/remotes \
    | sort -u | while read -r c; do GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" ls-tree -r "$c"; done \
    | awk -F '\t' -v re="$SPEC_RE" '{ split($1, m, " ") } m[2] == "blob" && $2 ~ re { print m[3] }' \
    | sort -u | GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" cat-file --batch-check='%(objectname)' 2>/dev/null | grep -vc missing || true)
[ "$have" = 0 ] || { echo "STOP: $have spec-side output or source file(s) reached through a branch (the records branch?) are in .git"; fail=1; }
if [ $fail -ne 0 ]; then echo "Tell the owner before doing anything else." >&2; exit 1; fi
echo "clean folder at $(git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --short HEAD); no spec-side files on disk or in .git"
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# The spec-side folders a clean folder leaves out (CONTRIBUTING.md,
# "Barriers"): the one list the barrier tools and their tests build these
# names from, since M3. Tab-separated: the folder, its kind (source:
# matched as a whole word or a path into it; transcripts: a path into it),
# the transcript check's rule ID (neutral numbers since M4b) and its label
# (sessions/REVIEWED.json names rules by label or ID, so a label never
# changes). The deny lists in config/claude/*.json are Claude Code's own
# syntax and keep their literal paths; C-UNIT checks they cover every
# folder here.
vendor/emulator	source	F-8	vendor/emulator/ (spec side)
harness	source	F-9	harness/ source (spec side)
sessions/spec	transcripts	F-11	spec-side session transcripts

You are the clean session for small-beeps (~/Development/[REDACTED:private]/clean). Same rules as always: the clean room, your role file, no spec-side folders, no stock or GPL firmware, the privacy rule for the public repo. Save this prompt unedited as docs/prompts/clean-pin-flags.md, archive the previous session's transcript, write this session's EXPOSURE entry.

0. Answers to your store-region questions (record them where the decisions live: DESIGN-NOTES / the guide / R-STORE-12):
   1. Yes. Moving on until there is room (at most once round) and 128 record parts are accepted. Every save the old code accepted writes the same bytes, and the power-cut runs cover the new path. Say plainly in STORE-FORMAT that only previously refused saves behave differently.
   2. Keep every extra refusal. The VM region stays refused: it holds the stock firmware's settings and is where an update stages its loader, so a store there could be lost or break an update. The refusal message should say why.
   3. Good. SR-11 waits for spec. Until it is answered, the guide's wording stands (survives fwtest and the app, not yet a real unit's update).
   4. Good.
   5. Fine: the golden is unchanged and the cause was a block edge. Add a note in the fmgold script saying key events must sit well clear of audio block edges, and why.
   6. 18 ms once at init is acceptable. Don't optimise it; record the figures in the guide's sizing section.

Pin it the same way 0.7.0 to 0.9.0 were pinned: one pull request on the clean side, the digest from the published image, C-HARNESS-IMAGE-REPRO and C-HARNESS-ISA green. Run the firmware suite on it. A case may now end as trap (exit code 6); if any of ours does, that's a finding, report it.

2. Refuse per-folder CPU and feature flags (amends BR-11). A firmware folder may still set its own -m flags for anything else, but its objects must be compiled for the SDK's CPU and float features: target CPU r3, and float features either +fprev1 or none. Use BR-13's own reading (note_cpu, clang -### for each compile line) rather than matching flag spellings, so -mcpu, -mfprev2, -msimd, -Xclang -target-feature and anything new are all caught the same way. The Plaits demo's +fprev1 stays allowed because it equals the SDK's set. Refuse at build time with a message that names the folder, the flag's effect (e.g. "double-precision float, which the SDK's flags exclude and fwtest doesn't run") and the fix. Add a seams test per refusal kind (another CPU, double precision, SIMD) and one that the allowed set passes. Update BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md (BR-11's section) and the requirements.

Separate pull requests for 1 and 2, each with CI green. Give me the merge order (after #173). Report briefly, then you're done.

content.content:
Done, ready to clear.

## Questions

1. **The store did not stay strictly "unchanged".** You said it works unchanged in any region of 3 sectors or more. It does, but your worked example didn't: with the old code, 16 sectors could keep only one rewritable 4 096-byte record beside the base's own records. Two changes fixed that:
   - The store now keeps moving to the next sector until it has room, at most once round. Every save the old code accepted makes exactly the same flash writes as before; only saves it used to refuse behave differently.
   - It now tracks 128 record parts instead of 32 (1.5 KiB of RAM). A 4 096-byte record is 9 parts, so 32 ran out at three such records.

   Is that acceptable?
2. **The build refuses more regions than the five you listed.** It also refuses regions over 128 sectors, in the boot area, in the stock firmware's VM region (its settings, and where an update stages its loader), the Bluetooth sector, and the per-unit last sector. HARDWARE-SPEC says a store must or should stay out of each of these. Should the VM region be allowed?
3. **SR-11 is filed.** HW-87 to HW-93 give where the app area starts, but no fixed end, so the build takes 0x94000 (the stock layout's end) as the conservative reading. The request also asks whether an update erases flash between our image and 0x94000. Until it's answered, the guide says a store there survives fwtest and the app, but not yet an update on a real unit. Returning a unit to the stock firmware erases it; the default region survives that.
4. **The PLAITS_HWFLOAT exception is gone.** The 68 write-back stores the check had counted in that build were all misreadings of a float instruction. With the right disassembly it has none. One narrow new allowance replaces it: the firmware suite's bad-instruction test build, which contains undecodable bytes on purpose.
5. **I changed one line of the fmgold test script, not its golden.** The last key release moved from 3950.0 to 3950.7 ms. At 3950.0 it sat within 10 µs of an audio block edge: on both main's image and the new one, 249.99 ms gave one output and 250.01 ms gave the golden. The new image is slightly bigger, its blocks run 0.011 ms later, and that tipped it over the edge.
6. **A full 16-sector region is slow at start-up: 18.1 ms in fwtest** with eleven 4 096-byte records. For comparison: 2.2 ms for one record in 5 sectors, 1.1 ms for today's region with the base's records and two small payloads. It happens once, in the firmware's init. Is that acceptable, or should I look at speeding it up?

## What was done

- **Setup:** the role file says `clean`. clean-1028's transcript is archived and `check-transcripts.py` passes (23 transcripts). The prompt is saved unedited as `docs/prompts/clean-store-region.md`, and this session's EXPOSURE entry is written. Disk was 6.1 GB free at the start and 4.5 GB at the lowest.
- **#172, BR-13:** the write-back check now disassembles each object with the CPU and float flags it was compiled with, and refuses any instruction it can't read. A float-heavy test object passes. Main's check wrongly refuses it, and the new check finds a real store planted after the float code. CI is green.
- **#173, the store region:**
  - A firmware sets `STORE_BASE` and `STORE_SIZE` in its own linker script; the default stays three sectors at 0xFC000.
  - The build checks both links and, for each bad region, says what's wrong and where one of that size would fit.
  - The guide has a "Where the store goes" section, with the sizing rule and a worked example: 16 sectors from 0x80000 for several 4 096-byte records.
  - DESIGN-NOTES, STORE-FORMAT and the requirements (new R-STORE-12) are updated, and SR-11 is filed.
  - Tests:
    - 402 unit tests pass, including one per refusal.
    - Power cuts run in 5 and 16 sectors: 724 cuts over five saves, never neither copy and never a mix.
    - Seams, firmware, ARP, package and preset suites pass (70 of 70 presets); perf passes every budget.

    CI is green.
  - CI's first run failed the emulator-terms check: two hex numbers (the example's start address and a test value) matched emulator-only terms. I replaced them.
- **One attempt that fetched nothing:** a `git archive main` needed a file this folder leaves out. Lazy fetching is off, so it stopped without downloading anything. It's recorded in EXPOSURE.

## Merge order

1. #172 (`build/disasm-flags`)
2. #173 (`store/region`, which contains #172's commits)

**First in the merge order.** Three commits: the session's start (clean-1027's transcript archived, this session's prompt and EXPOSURE entry), the pin, and a note in PLAN.md.

**What:** `config/fwtest-image` moves to fwtest 0.9.0's digest (`sha256:49ad9617…bd5c`), published from main when #162 merged. Also: PLAN.md's real-hardware level notes USB MIDI as a class-compliant device for firmwares built on small-beeps (BR-10), under M11.

**Why:** the owner's prompt for this session, sections 0, 1 and 3; R-SEP-3. 0.9.0 keeps the old value for a store with write-back into its own base register (SR-10). A unit has no MIDI OUT jack (HW-67), so USB MIDI is how MIDI out reaches a computer or an iPad. There is nothing to build for it now.

**How:** the digest comes from the push step of the image workflow's run on `f9a9bc64` (its digest and version lines only). Main's image (build A at `f9a9bc64`) ran three suites, once on 0.8.0 and once on 0.9.0, each from a copy of the tree: the firmware suite (the store's cases included), the ARP suite, and the seams suite (whose store case covers the firmware kinds' store). The output trees were then compared file by file.

**Result:**
- All three suites PASS on both versions. `tests/test_store.py` OK.
- **No output changed.** 3 641 files were compared: the firmware suite's 3 089, the ARP suite's 391 and the seams suite's 161.
- The 668 files that differ hold only fwtest's version (`result.json`) and the runner (`runner.txt`), plus the seams suite's seven build logs, which show their copies' paths. Every image the seams suite built is byte-identical.
- Seen on the way: #157's merge (`c298dcf9`) also pushed an image reporting 0.8.0, digest `e62c0383…`, not the pinned 0.8.0 `99c22231…`. This is the same pattern #152 saw for 0.7.0. Nothing here uses it; it is a question in the session report.

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 0 | power-cut | Ran to `--power-cut`, and every golden file matched. `detail` names the erase or program the cut interrupted, if any, and how many of its bytes were done. |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks), or it ran or read the code window while the flash chip was busy ("The flash chip"). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |
| 6 | trap | A core executed `bkpt`, the compiler's `__builtin_trap` (since 0.10.0; before, a fault). `detail` names the core and the pc of the `bkpt`. The run ends there. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 6, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 too. A suite case may
expect `trap`. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1

---
name: suites-from-snapshot
description: "Clean side: run the long fwtest suites from an rsync copy of the tree, one at a time, with tools/find-python.sh's Python"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Run the firmware, ARP, preset, package and Plaits suites from a copy of the working tree (`rsync -a --exclude .git --exclude out`) in the job's tmp folder, never from the live tree, and one heavy run at a time.

**Why:** clean-a1-packager voided a suite run by switching branches mid-build. In clean-1027 a firmware suite run alongside other fwtest runs was killed by SIGTERM part way and had to be rerun. Also, a `sh` script finds an x86 `/usr/local/bin/python3` that fails with "Bad CPU type"; `sh tools/find-python.sh` gives the working one (`/usr/bin/python3`).

**How to apply:** wait for the copy to finish before changing branches. Unit tests that need `.git` (test_private) fail in the copy, so run C-UNIT in the real tree. Related: [[ci-artifacts-named-files]].
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""tools/fwtest runs an image pinned by digest (R-SEP-3, R-HARN-10; check
C-FWTEST-PIN).

  check-fwtest-pin.py

config/fwtest-image must hold one image reference of the form
`ghcr.io/<owner>/<repository>@sha256:<64 hex digits>`, with no quiet words
in it (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Low profile"), or `unpublished` until the first
image is published (tools/fwtest then refuses to run). tools/fwtest must
take the image from that file, check for the digest form, and run it with
no network, as linux/amd64, with the working folder mounted read-only.
"""
import os
import re
import sys

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
REF = re.compile(r"^ghcr\.io/[a-z0-9-]+/[a-z0-9._-]+@sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$")
QUIET = re.compile(r"fm-?1|m-?vave|jie-?li|synth|firmware", re.I)
WRAPPER_MUST = [
    'PIN_FILE="$ROOT/config/fwtest-image"',
    "*@sha256:" + "?" * 64 + ")",
    "--network none",
    "--platform linux/amd64",
    ':/work:ro"',
]


def pinned(text):
    lines = [l.strip() for l in text.splitlines() if l.strip() and not l.startswith("#")]
    return lines[0] if len(lines) == 1 else None


def check(root=ROOT):
    problems = []
    with open(os.path.join(root, "config", "fwtest-image"), encoding="utf-8") as f:
        ref = pinned(f.read())

2723:### 2026-10-26 M8b: presets 65 to 70
2768:### 2026-10-27 clean-1027: seams for firmwares built on small-beeps
3177:### 2026-10-28 clean-1028: saves that survive a power cut (BR-12, R-STORE-11)
3301:### 2026-10-28 clean-1028: per-folder compiler flags (BR-11, R-BUILD-5)

3420:### 2026-10-28 clean-store-region: each firmware chooses its own store region (R-STORE-12)
  after any image; 768 bytes of RAM), and a sector's "holds a firmware
  kind" flag, a 32-bit mask until now (32 sectors at most), is a byte a
  sector. The ring's next sector is a compare, not a modulo (no divide at
  run time). The test engine's linker scripts `store5.ld` and
  `store16.ld` are the documented way, used.
- **The build refuses what doesn't fit** (`tools/store-region.pl`, run by
  `tools/build.sh` on both links, `app.elf` and `app-pkg.elf`, whose
  image is the longer by the app area's 0x120-byte directory): a start
  off a 4 KiB sector boundary or a size not whole sectors; fewer than 3
  sectors (the store's minimum: a head, a sector to move on to, and one
  to compact) or more than `STORE_SECTORS_MAX`; a region over the image
  (window address `0x02000000 + n` is chip offset `0x4000 + n`, HW-5,
  HW-91) or the boot area; a region across the app area's end, or in the
  stock layout past it (the VM region, the Bluetooth sector, the stock
  user patch region, the per-unit last sector: HW-80). Each message says
  what is wrong, with the numbers, and where a region of that size would
  fit (from the first sector after the image to the last start that ends
  by the app area's end, and the unused region's 3 sectors). The checks
  are in a script, not ld `ASSERT`s, because an `ASSERT`'s message can't
  carry numbers, and an `ASSERT` would stop the link before the script
  could say more; platform.ld's two store asserts are gone.
- **Stricter than asked, where HW-80 says so.** The owner named five
  refusals (over the image, across the app area's end, the stock user
  patch region, off a sector boundary, below the store's minimum). The
  build also refuses: more than the store keeps track of (an array
  bound, so a must), the boot area, and the stock layout's regions past
  the app area that aren't the unused one, the VM region (the stock
  firmware's settings, and where an update stages its loader), the
  Bluetooth sector and the last sector (never to be erased). HW-80 says a
  store "must stay out of" or "should stay out of" each.
- **Where the app area ends: a reading, SR-11.** HW-87 to HW-93 give the
  app area's start (`0x4000`) and its length as its area head says (our
  packager's: our app's), not a fixed end; HW-80 gives the stock
  layout's, `0x93FFF`. The build takes `0x94000` as the end, the most
  conservative reading that leaves the owner's example (a region in the
  space a stock image would take, after our smaller one) possible.
  SR-11 asks the spec side where the area may end, whether the chip's
  loader or an update touches flash past our package's image, and
  whether the window's decryption reaches there.
- **The store's room-making moves on more than once.** With the region
  free, the worked example (16 sectors for several 4 096-byte records)
  showed what bigger regions need. The ring made room by moving the head
  on once: open the next sector, copy the live records of the one after
  it into it (compaction), and, if what was left was still too small,
  refuse. With large payloads most sectors are mostly live, so one move
  often frees nothing: in the model, 16 sectors kept only one rewritable
  4 096-byte payload beside the base's full store in every history (two
  alone), though they have room for twelve. `make_room` (and the model's
  `_room`) now moves on while the new head has no room, once round the
  ring at most, each move an erase of a sector holding nothing live and
  a copy of the next's live records, as before; still `STORE_ERR_FULL`
  when the sector to move to holds something live. A save that one move
  served makes exactly the commands it made before (the loop only goes
  on where the old code refused), so every history the store took before
  is unchanged. The cost: in a nearly full region one save can erase
  several sectors (in the power-cut case's save, 2 for one part; up to 7
  seen in the model's searches), still spread over the ring.
- **More parts kept track of.** `STORE_FW_KEYS`, the places for parts,
  was 32: three 4 096-byte payloads (9 parts each) left no room for a
  rewrite of one, in any region. It is 128 (1.5 KiB more RAM): 14 such
  payloads, 13 beside a rewrite. Past it a write is refused as full, as
  before. `STORE_FW_PAYLOADS` (32 payloads) stays.
- **Start-up grows with what the region holds.** `store_init` reads
  every sector's header, every valid sector whole, and those holding a
  firmware kind's record twice more (BR-12). Measured in fwtest (the
  store record's `init_ticks`): the default region holding the base's
  full store, a 10-byte and a 1 500-byte payload, 1.13 ms (the base's own
  records alone: 0.28 ms, clean-1028); 5 sectors holding the base's full
  store and a 4 096-byte payload, 2.17 ms; 16 sectors holding the base's
  full store and eleven 4 096-byte payloads after 27 rewrites, 18.1 ms.
  The larger key table is about 1 % of it (2.14 ms in 5 sectors with 32
  places). A firmware calls `store_init` once, in its init.
- **The sizing rule, plainly.** A rewrite is atomic (BR-12), so it needs
  room for the old payload and the new one at once: everything live plus
  the new payload's records must fit in the region's sectors but one, at
  4 080 bytes of records a sector (`(STORE_SECTORS - 1) * 4 080`, the
  check `put_fw` makes before writing anything), with no record across
  two sectors, and its parts within the places for parts. A payload of
  n bytes is `ceil(n / 492)` parts of 512 bytes as records (the last
  smaller); 4 096 bytes take 4 288. The ring's layout takes some of that
  room back, so what fits in every history is less; from the model
  (`tools/store.py`), histories as clean-1028's table describes them;
  this session's script, run on main's model, gives that table's figures
  for 3 and 5 sectors (3 920, 1 664 and never; 5 904, 4 948 and every
  one) and for 4 gives 4 904, 3 268 (the table: 3 300) and never, so the
  "before" figures below are its own:

  | Region | One payload alone, rewritten 40 times | One payload beside the base's full store and a small payload (100 histories) | A 4 096-byte payload beside the base's full store (300 histories) | 4 096-byte payloads, each rewritable: alone (beside the base's full store; 100 histories in 16 sectors, 300 in 5) |
  |-------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|
  | 3 sectors (the default) | 3 920 bytes | 2 444 bytes (1 664 before) | never | none |
  | 4 sectors | 5 396 (4 904 before) | 4 284 (3 268) | every one (never) | 1 (1) |
  | 5 sectors | 5 904 | 5 904 (4 948) | every one | 2 (2) (1 (1) before) |
  | 16 sectors | 5 904 | 5 904 | every one | 12 (11) (2 (1) before) |

  So a 4 096-byte payload now needs 4 sectors beside the base's full
  store, where clean-1028 found 5. The store's format is unchanged
  (docs/STORE-FORMAT.md): a region of any size from 3 sectors up is the
  same ring of the same sectors.
- **Tested.** C-UNIT: `tests/test_store_region.py`, each refusal on the
  check's own input (the symbols `nm` prints), with its message and the
  place it offers, the default and both test regions taken, every

  user patch region, the per-unit last sector: HW-80). Each message says
  what is wrong, with the numbers, and where a region of that size would
  fit (from the first sector after the image to the last start that ends
  by the app area's end, and the unused region's 3 sectors). The checks
  are in a script, not ld `ASSERT`s, because an `ASSERT`'s message can't
  carry numbers, and an `ASSERT` would stop the link before the script
  could say more; platform.ld's two store asserts are gone.
- **Stricter than asked, where HW-80 says so.** The owner named five
  refusals (over the image, across the app area's end, the stock user
  patch region, off a sector boundary, below the store's minimum). The
  build also refuses: more than the store keeps track of (an array
  bound, so a must), the boot area, and the stock layout's regions past
  the app area that aren't the unused one, the VM region (the stock
  firmware's settings, and where an update stages its loader), the
  Bluetooth sector and the last sector (never to be erased). HW-80 says a
  store "must stay out of" or "should stay out of" each.
- **Where the app area ends: a reading, SR-11.** HW-87 to HW-93 give the
  app area's start (`0x4000`) and its length as its area head says (our
  packager's: our app's), not a fixed end; HW-80 gives the stock
  layout's, `0x93FFF`. The build takes `0x94000` as the end, the most
  conservative reading that leaves the owner's example (a region in the
  space a stock image would take, after our smaller one) possible.
  SR-11 asks the spec side where the area may end, whether the chip's
  loader or an update touches flash past our package's image, and
  whether the window's decryption reaches there.
- **The store's room-making moves on more than once.** With the region
  free, the worked example (16 sectors for several 4 096-byte records)
  showed what bigger regions need. The ring made room by moving the head
  on once: open the next sector, copy the live records of the one after
  it into it (compaction), and, if what was left was still too small,
  refuse. With large payloads most sectors are mostly live, so one move
  often frees nothing: in the model, 16 sectors kept only one rewritable
  4 096-byte payload beside the base's full store in every history (two
  alone), though they have room for twelve. `make_room` (and the model's
  `_room`) now moves on while the new head has no room, once round the
  ring at most, each move an erase of a sector holding nothing live and
  a copy of the next's live records, as before; still `STORE_ERR_FULL`
  when the sector to move to holds something live. A save that one move
  served makes exactly the commands it made before (the loop only goes
  on where the old code refused), so every history the store took before
  is unchanged. The cost: in a nearly full region one save can erase
  several sectors (in the power-cut case's save, 2 for one part; up to 7
  seen in the model's searches), still spread over the ring.
- **More parts kept track of.** `STORE_FW_KEYS`, the places for parts,
  was 32: three 4 096-byte payloads (9 parts each) left no room for a
  rewrite of one, in any region. It is 128 (1.5 KiB more RAM): 14 such
  payloads, 13 beside a rewrite. Past it a write is refused as full, as
  before. `STORE_FW_PAYLOADS` (32 payloads) stays.
- **Start-up grows with what the region holds.** `store_init` reads
  every sector's header, every valid sector whole, and those holding a
  firmware kind's record twice more (BR-12). Measured in fwtest (the
  store record's `init_ticks`): the default region holding the base's
  full store, a 10-byte and a 1 500-byte payload, 1.13 ms (the base's own
  records alone: 0.28 ms, clean-1028); 5 sectors holding the base's full
  store and a 4 096-byte payload, 2.17 ms; 16 sectors holding the base's
  full store and eleven 4 096-byte payloads after 27 rewrites, 18.1 ms.
  The larger key table is about 1 % of it (2.14 ms in 5 sectors with 32

  room for the old payload and the new one at once: everything live plus

content.content:
The build checks the region on both links (the raw image and the
package's, whose image is 0x120 bytes longer) and prints it, here for an
image of about 110 KiB:

```
app.elf: store region 0x80000 to 0x8FFFF, 16 sectors (the image ends at 0x1F7C7)
app-pkg.elf: store region 0x80000 to 0x8FFFF, 16 sectors (the image ends at 0x1F8E7)
```

It refuses a region, saying what is wrong and where one of that size
would fit, if it:

- doesn't start on a 4 KiB sector boundary, or isn't whole sectors;
- is smaller than 3 sectors (the store's minimum) or larger than 128
  (`STORE_SECTORS_MAX`, what the store keeps track of);
- overlaps your image (it starts at chip offset `0x4000`), or the boot
  area below it;
- crosses the end of the app area at `0x94000`, or lies past it in the
  stock layout: the VM region (`0x94000` to `0xE8FFF`), the Bluetooth
  sector, the stock user patch region, or the chip's last sector (its
  per-unit key, which must never be erased).

So a region goes either in the app area after your image, or in the
unused three sectors. `0x94000` is where the stock layout's app area
ends (HW-80); the hardware facts give the app area's start but no fixed
end, so this is the conservative reading until SR-11 is answered. For
example, 5 sectors from `0x10000` with the same image:

```
app.elf: store region: the region (0x10000 to 0x14FFF) overlaps the image, which ends at chip offset 0x1F7C7: start it at 0x20000 or later
app.elf: store region: where it would fit: a region of 5 sectors fits in the app area after the image, from 0x20000 to 0x8F000 at the latest; the unused region 0xFC000 to 0xFEFFF holds 3 (the default, STORE_BASE 0xFC000, STORE_SIZE 0x3000)
FAIL: the store's region doesn't fit (above; tools/store-region.pl)
```

How large: saves are atomic, so a rewrite needs room for the old payload
and the new one beside everything else live. The rule: everything live
plus the new payload's records must fit in the region's sectors but one
(the ring keeps one free to move on), each sector holding 4 080 bytes
of records, a part's record (512 bytes for a full one) never split
across two; a 4 096-byte payload is 9 parts, 4 288 bytes as records. In
practice, from the store's model (`tools/store.py`) over random
histories:

| Region | One payload, alone: the largest | One payload beside the base's full store | 4 096-byte payloads, each rewritable: alone (beside the base's full store) |
|-------:|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| 3 sectors (the default) | 3 920 bytes | 2 444 bytes | none |
| 4 sectors | 5 396 | 4 284 | 1 (1) |
| 5 sectors | 5 904 (the most a payload takes) | 5 904 | 2 (2) |
| 16 sectors | 5 904 | 5 904 | 12 (11) |

**A worked example: 16 sectors for several 4 096-byte records.** Say your
firmware keeps eight 4 096-byte records (kinds `0x80`, ids 0 to 7: a
bank of samples, say) and rewrites any of them at any time. Today's
three sectors can't rewrite even one. Sixteen sectors (64 KiB) keep
twelve, each rewritable, so eight leaves room to grow. Put them where
your image can grow into the space below them: high in the app area,
from `0x80000` (the script above), they leave your image room to grow to
496 KiB (it starts at `0x4000`), and 64 KiB of the app area above them
free; the build will refuse the region the day the image reaches it. Everything else is as before:

```c
for (id = 0; id < 8; id++)
    n = store_get(0x80, id, rec, sizeof rec, &version);   /* at start-up */
r = store_put(0x80, id, 1, rec, 4096);                    /* from your serve */
```

A larger region costs some time: `store_init` reads every sector, and
those holding your kinds' records three times, so with eleven 4 096-byte
payloads in 16 sectors it takes 18 ms (in fwtest; 2.2 ms for one in 5
sectors, 1.1 ms for today's three holding the base's records and two
small payloads). Call it once, in your init, before the audio starts.
And a save in a nearly full region may move the ring on several sectors
(an erase each, up to 12 ms on the chip, HW-77) before it has room. Three
things to know about a region in the app area:

- It is yours from the first start: the store finds it erased (or
  holding what it holds) and formats sectors as it needs them. Moving the
  region later starts an empty store; nothing moves your data for you.
- Your own `.fwsc` package writes nothing past your image (section 6),
  but whether an update erases the rest of the app area is not yet known
  (SR-11). Until it is answered, treat a store there as surviving your
  own builds in fwtest and the app, not yet as surviving an update on a
  unit.
- The stock firmware's package covers the whole app area (`0x00000` to
  `0x93FFF`, HW-80), so returning a unit to the stock firmware erases a
  store there; the default region survives it.

## 4. Your records in RAM

Tests read state at fixed RAM addresses. The platform keeps its records
at the start of RAM (`base/firmware/platform.ld`) and keeps two places
for an engine's:

- the engine's slot, `0x01C00590`: one record of at most 64 bytes, in
  section `.beacon.engine0`;
- after the store's record, from `0x01C00870`: sections

content.content:
passed over too and counted. Of the records with the same kind and id,
the one with the highest sequence number counts; then every record older
than the newest reset is void. A record of a kind or id the reader does
not know is counted and otherwise ignored, and never copied forward.

## Writing

A firmware kind's payload (since clean-1028) is refused before anything is
written if the store has no place for it or its parts, or if everything
live and the new write's records together would not fit in the region's
sectors but one (each sector less its header); otherwise its parts are
appended in order, each as below, the last only once the others read
back. A write refused part way (the ring's layout left no room) leaves
the old payload: its new parts are not live.

A record is appended in the head after its last byte that is not erased,
programmed in one go (a page program for each 256-byte page it touches),
and read back. Nothing written is ever written again: a record replaces
an older one only by being newer.

When the head has no room, the next sector in the ring becomes the head:
it is erased, and its header written with the next sequence number. Then
every record still live in the sector after the new head (the oldest) is
copied into the new head, with a new sequence number, so that sector holds
nothing live by the time the ring comes round to erase it. If a sector
can't be freed without losing a live record, the write is refused and
nothing is written.

## Other regions

A region of another size or place (R-STORE-12) has the same format: the
same ring of the same sectors, sector 0 at `STORE_BASE`. The test
engine's own regions (`tests/seams/engine/store5.ld` and `store16.ld`) are
5 and 16 sectors from `0x20000`. `tools/store.py` takes a region's size in
sectors and its base (`store.py show FLASH.bin --region BASE SECTORS`).
Until clean-store-region a test build, `SB_TEST_STORE_WIDE`, gave the store
5 sectors from `0xFA000`; the build now refuses that region, two of its
sectors being the stock firmware's user patch region.

262:## 4. Your records in RAM
288:## 5. Build
351:## 6. Test with fwtest, run in the app
387:## 7. MIDI out
423:## 8. Keeping up with the base

programmed in one go (a page program for each 256-byte page it touches),
and read back. Nothing written is ever written again: a record replaces
an older one only by being newer.

When the head has no room, the next sector in the ring becomes the head:
it is erased, and its header written with the next sequence number. Then
every record still live in the sector after the new head (the oldest) is
copied into the new head, with a new sequence number, so that sector holds
nothing live by the time the ring comes round to erase it. If a sector
can't be freed without losing a live record, the write is refused and
nothing is written.

## Other regions

A region of another size or place (R-STORE-12) has the same format: the
same ring of the same sectors, sector 0 at `STORE_BASE`. The test
engine's own regions (`tests/seams/engine/store5.ld` and `store16.ld`) are
5 and 16 sectors from `0x20000`. `tools/store.py` takes a region's size in
sectors and its base (`store.py show FLASH.bin --region BASE SECTORS`).
Until clean-store-region a test build, `SB_TEST_STORE_WIDE`, gave the store
5 sectors from `0xFA000`; the build now refuses that region, two of its
sectors being the stock firmware's user patch region.

# base source (a path from the repository's root, under firmware/) out
# of the build, so a firmware can replace it or do without it. A
# firmware built on the base calls this script from the base's folder
# (docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md).
#
# Per-folder flags (BR-11): --cflags DIR FLAGS adds FLAGS, after the
# base's own, to every C file under DIR, a --src folder or a folder in
# one; --cxxflags to its C++, --asflags to its assembly. Repeatable; a
# file under several such folders gets each one's flags in the order
# given (so a folder inside another can override it, -O2 after -O0, say).
# The base's own files, its runtime included, are always built with the
# base's flags. FLAGS are words of A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and _ = + . , / : -;
# a relative path in -I, -isystem or -iquote (joined to it: -Iinclude)
# is from DIR. Only these families are taken: -D, -U, -O, -W, -w, -f,
# -m, -std=, -I, -isystem, -iquote, -g, -pedantic, -ansi; and of them
# not those that would reach the host, the outputs' determinism or
# another tool: an absolute path or one with "..", -fdebug-prefix-map
# and its kin, -fprofile..., -fplugin..., -fpass-plugin...,
# -fsave-optimization-record, -Wa, -Wp, -Wl (check_flags).
#
# The platform (BR-2): --platform leaves out the base's instrument, the
# files below, defines SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL (firmware/src/engine.h) and
# links with firmware/platform.ld, whose assertions cover only the
# platform's records; --ld SCRIPT links with a script of one's own
# instead (in the base or in a --src folder), which includes platform.ld
# (INCLUDE platform.ld) and asserts its own records.
set -eu

INSTRUMENT="firmware/src/arp.c firmware/src/fm.c firmware/src/fm_play.c
            firmware/src/patches.c firmware/src/saving.c firmware/src/spectrum.c firmware/src/views.c"

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
PLATFORM=linux/amd64

sha256() {
    if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1
    else shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; fi
}

}

cmd_build() {
    out="" src_mount=/mnt/small-beeps-src defines="" demo="" mounts="" srcs="" leave="" n=0
    platform="" ldscript="" ff=""
    while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        case "$1" in
            --out) out=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --platform) platform=1; shift ;;
            --ld)
                [ -f "$2" ] || { echo "build: --ld $2: no such file" >&2; exit 2; }
                ldscript="$(cd "$(dirname "$2")" && pwd)/$(basename "$2")"; shift 2 ;;
            --src)
                [ -d "$2" ] || { echo "build: --src $2 is not a folder" >&2; exit 2; }
                d=$(cd "$2" && pwd)
                case "$ROOT/" in
                    "$d"/*) echo "build: --src $2 holds the base itself; give the folders of your own sources" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                case "$d/" in
                    "$ROOT/firmware/"*) echo "build: --src $2 is inside firmware/, which is built already" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                    *" "*) echo "build: --src $2: a path with a space is not supported" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                n=$((n + 1))
                srcs="$srcs $d"
                shift 2 ;;
            --cflags|--cxxflags|--asflags)
                [ $# -ge 3 ] || { echo "build: $1 takes a folder and its flags" >&2; exit 2; }
                [ -d "$2" ] || { echo "build: $1 $2 is not a folder" >&2; exit 2; }
                check_flags "$1" "$3"
                ff="$ff;${1#--}|$(cd "$2" && pwd)|$3"; shift 3 ;;
            --leave-out)
                case "$2" in
                    firmware/*) [ -f "$ROOT/$2" ] || { echo "build: --leave-out $2: no such base file" >&2; exit 2; } ;;
                    *) echo "build: --leave-out takes a base source's path from the repository's root (firmware/...)" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                leave="$leave $2"; shift 2 ;;
            --src-mount) src_mount=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --define)
                case "$2" in
                    ''|*[!A-Z0-9_]*) echo "build: --define takes a NAME of A-Z, 0-9 and _" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                defines="$defines $2"; shift 2 ;;
            --demo)

sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld
```

| Option | What |
|--------|------|
| `--platform` | leaves out the base's instrument (its FM engine, presets, arpeggiator, screens and saving), builds with `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL`, links with `platform.ld` |
| `--src DIR` | every `.c`, `.S` and `.cc` under DIR, built with the firmware's flags and `-I DIR`; repeat it for more folders (not a folder holding `base/`) |
| `--ld SCRIPT` | your linker script (in `base/` or in a `--src` folder) |
| `--define NAME` | `-DNAME` for every source (yours and the base's) |
| `--leave-out FILE` | a base source left out (`firmware/src/...`), to replace it with your own |
| `--cflags DIR FLAGS` | FLAGS for the C files under DIR (a `--src` folder or a folder inside one), after the firmware's flags; the base's own files never get them |
| `--cxxflags DIR FLAGS` | the same for the C++ (`.cc`) files under DIR |
| `--asflags DIR FLAGS` | the same for the assembly (`.S`) files under DIR |

**Flags for your own folders.** Your code can have flags of its own, folder
by folder, while the base's files keep the base's (R-BUILD-5):

```sh
sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld \
    --cflags src "-DMY_BOARD=2 -Wno-sign-compare" \
    --cflags src/vendor/dsp "-O2 -w -Iinclude" \
    --cxxflags src "-std=c++17"
```

- A file gets the flags of every folder it is under, in the order you
  gave them, after the firmware's own (so `-O2` here replaces the
  firmware's `-Os` for `src/vendor/dsp`, and its `-w` silences the
  warnings the firmware's `-Werror` would stop on).
- `--cflags` is for `.c` files only, `--cxxflags` for `.cc`, `--asflags`
  for `.S` (which are run through the preprocessor, so `-D` works there).
- A path in `-I`, `-isystem` or `-iquote` is from the folder the flags are
  for, and is joined to it: `-Iinclude`, not `-I include`.
- Taken: `-D`, `-U`, `-O`, `-W`, `-w`, `-f`, `-m`, `-std=`, `-I`,
  `-isystem`, `-iquote`, `-g`, `-pedantic`, `-ansi`, as words of letters,
  digits and `_ = + . , / : -`. Refused, so the build stays deterministic
  and inside its container: absolute paths and `..`, `-fdebug-prefix-map`
  and its kin, `-fprofile...`, `-fplugin...`, `-Wa,`, `-Wp,`, `-Wl,`,
  and anything else (`-o`, `-c`, `-x`, `-include`, `-target`, `@file`, ...).
- `--define NAME` stays the way to set something for every file, the
  base's included.

The outputs, in `out/`:

- `app.bin`: the raw image (linked at `0x02000000`), what fwtest and the
  app run;
- `app-pkg.bin`: the same code linked at `0x02000120`, for a `.fwsc`
  package (section 6);
- `app.elf`, `app-pkg.elf`: with symbols, for finding things;
- `app.size`: code, data, RAM and stack in bytes;
- `SHA256SUMS`.

cd ~/Development/[REDACTED:private]/clean && cat >> docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md <<'EOF'

### 2026-10-29 clean-pin-flags: a folder's code for the SDK's CPU and float (amends BR-11, R-BUILD-5)

BR-11 let a `--src` folder set its own `-m` flags, so a folder could
build for another CPU or with instructions the SDK's flags leave out
(double-precision float, SIMD): code fwtest doesn't run (it runs the
forms `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1` give, R-HARN-14) and the chip may not either.
The owner's rule: a folder may still set other `-m` flags, but its
objects are built for CPU `r3`, with the features `+fprev1` or none.

- **By clang's reading, not by spelling.** BR-13 already reads each
  compile line's CPU and features from clang's own `-###` line
  (`note_cpu`, now `read_cpu` and `note_cpu`). The check takes the same
  reading of every folder file's flags (the base's for its kind, then
  its folders'), so `-mcpu=r4`, `-mfprev2`, `-msimd`, `-mcordic`, a
  `-target-feature` and a flag the toolchain gains later are caught
  alike. The toolchain's target knows CPUs `generic`, `r1` to `r5` with
  variants (`r3s`, `r3v1`, ...) and the features `cordic`, `fprev1`,
  `fprev2` (float and double), `full-rep`, `instrev1`, `instrev2`,
  `round-64`, `secext` and `simd` (its `-mcpu=help`).
- **What passes.** CPU exactly `r3` (not `r3s` or another variant), and
  of the features, each taken at its last `+` or `-`, none enabled but
  `fprev1`. So the base's own set, `-mfprev1` again, and
  `-mno-fprev1` (no float instructions: soft-float, which the base's
  runtime provides) all pass; the face-value reading of "+fprev1 or
  none". A reading with no CPU (clang read none) is refused too.
- **Where.** Only `--src` folders' files that have folder flags: the
  base's own files keep the base's flags, and two of the base's builds
  read without a CPU on purpose (the runtime's C and the Plaits demo,
  which are soft-float; the demo's `PLAITS_HWFLOAT` build adds `+fprev1`
  through `-Xclang -target-feature`, the SDK's set, and stays as it is).
- **When.** Every folder file is checked before any is compiled, so the
  refusal comes before a compiler error and once per option, folder and
  effect ("and N more" files), on stderr only. The message names the
  option and the folder as the user gave them (carried into the
  container beside the mount path; only messages see it, so the outputs
  stay the same from any place), the first file, what the flag does,
  which of the folder's flags alone give it (or "these flags together")
  and the fix.
- **`-Xclang`.** The owner named `-Xclang -target-feature` among the
  spellings to catch. A folder can't give it: `check_flags` takes only
  the listed families, and `-Xclang` is not one (refused at exit 2
  since clean-1028). The reading would catch it if it ever got through;
  its reading (`+fprev2`, the same as `-mfprev2`'s) is in the unit test.
  Through `-m`, `-mllvm` passes options to the code generator; none of
  the toolchain's changes the CPU or features (`-mllvm -mattr=...` is
  not one it knows), and any that did would show in the reading only if
  clang's driver saw it, so `-mllvm` is noted here as the remaining
  route.
- **Tested.** C-UNIT (`tests/test_build_flags.py`): the verdict on the
  readings of the SDK's set, `-mcpu=r3` alone, `-mno-fprev1`, another
  CPU, no CPU, double precision, SIMD and an unlisted feature. C-SEAMS
  (case flags): the flags folder built with `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`,
  `-mno-fprev1` (inner/, read as without float instructions), C++
  `-mfprev1` and assembly `-mcpu=r3`; and refused, each before any of
  its files is compiled, with its message: inner/ `-mcpu=r4`, the C++
  `-O2 -mfprev2` (only `-mfprev2` named) and the assembly `-msimd`.
EOF
echo ok
